notes.summary:
Computer fundamentals gives 4 to 6 direct questions in Tier 2. The most asked areas are the generations of computers, the CPU and its registers, RAM, ROM and cache, storage devices, data units and address lines, input and output devices, and number system conversions.

Most questions are one-line facts, so learn the tables below. The only working questions are unit conversions, address lines and base conversions.

concepts.title: What a computer is
concepts.body:
A computer takes input, processes it, stores it and gives output. This is the IPO cycle (input, process, output) with storage added.

  • Hardware: the parts you can touch (keyboard, CPU, monitor).
  • Software: the programs that tell hardware what to do.
  • Firmware: software stored permanently in hardware, like the BIOS in ROM.
  • Data is raw facts; information is processed, meaningful data.

The CPU (central processing unit) is called the brain of the computer. The motherboard is the main circuit board that connects everything.

concepts.title: History and generations
concepts.body:
GenerationYears (approx.)Main technologyExamples and notes
First1940–1956Vacuum tubesENIAC, UNIVAC; machine language; huge, hot, used punched cards
Second1956–1963TransistorsIBM 1401; assembly language, early high-level languages (FORTRAN, COBOL)
Third1964–1971Integrated circuits (IC)IBM System/360; keyboards, monitors and operating systems
Fourth1971–presentMicroprocessor (VLSI)Intel 4004 (1971), personal computers, GUIs
FifthPresent and futureArtificial intelligence, ULSI, parallel processingNatural language, robotics, expert systems
  • Charles Babbage is the father of the computer (Difference Engine, Analytical Engine). Ada Lovelace is called the first programmer.
  • Abacus is the earliest counting tool. Pascaline was Blaise Pascal's adding machine. Herman Hollerith used punched cards for the 1890 US census.
  • ENIAC (1946) was the first general-purpose electronic computer, built by Eckert and Mauchly. John von Neumann gave the stored-program idea.
  • PARAM 8000 (1991, C-DAC) was India's first supercomputer.

concepts.title: Types of computers
concepts.body:
By size and powerWhat it is
SupercomputerFastest; weather forecasting, research. Speed in FLOPS. Examples: PARAM, Frontier.
MainframeServes hundreds of users at once; banks, railways.
MinicomputerMid-sized, for a department or small firm.
MicrocomputerPersonal computer built around a microprocessor: desktop, laptop, tablet, smartphone.
  • A laptop is also called a notebook. A palmtop or PDA fits in the hand.
  • By how data is handled: analog (continuous data, like a speedometer), digital (discrete 0 and 1), hybrid (both, like ICU machines).
  • A server provides services to other computers (clients); a workstation is a powerful single-user computer.

concepts.title: CPU, registers and the bus
concepts.body:
The CPU has three main parts:

  • ALU (arithmetic logic unit): does maths (+, −) and logic (AND, OR, comparisons).
  • CU (control unit): fetches instructions, decodes them and directs the other parts. It does not process data itself.
  • Registers: tiny, fastest storage inside the CPU.
RegisterWhat it holds
PC (program counter)Address of the next instruction
IR (instruction register)The instruction being executed now
MAR (memory address register)Address of the memory location being accessed (the active memory location)
MDR / MBR (memory data / buffer register)Data being read from or written to memory
Accumulator (AC)Intermediate results of the ALU
  • The CPU runs the machine cycle: fetch, decode, execute, store.
  • Clock speed is measured in hertz (GHz today). A multi-core CPU has several processing cores on one chip.
  • A bus is a set of wires: the address bus carries addresses (one-way), the data bus carries data (two-way) and the control bus carries signals.

concepts.title: Booting
concepts.body:
• Booting is starting the computer and loading the operating system into RAM.
  • Cold boot: switching on from power off. Warm boot: restarting a running computer (Restart, or Ctrl+Alt+Del in older systems).
  • Steps: power on, the BIOS (or UEFI) in ROM runs the POST (power-on self-test) to check the hardware, then the bootstrap loader loads the operating system.
  • BIOS = Basic Input/Output System. CMOS is a small battery-backed memory that keeps BIOS settings and the date and time.

concepts.title: Primary memory: RAM, ROM and cache
concepts.body:
RAMROM
Full formRandom Access MemoryRead Only Memory
Volatile?Yes: loses data when power goesNo: keeps data
UsePrograms and data in use nowFirmware such as BIOS
Read/writeBothMostly read
  • SRAM (static): made of flip-flops, faster, costlier, no refresh needed; used for cache.
  • DRAM (dynamic): made of capacitors, must be refreshed again and again; used for main memory.
  • ROM types: PROM (written once by the user), EPROM (erased by ultraviolet light), EEPROM (erased electrically; flash memory is a kind of EEPROM).
  • Cache memory sits between CPU and RAM. It keeps the current programs and data ready so the CPU runs faster.
  • Virtual memory: part of the hard disk used as if it were RAM.

Memory hierarchy, fastest and costliest first: registers, cache, RAM, SSD, hard disk, optical disc, magnetic tape. Speed and cost per byte fall as you go down; capacity rises.

concepts.title: Secondary storage
concepts.body:
Secondary storage is non-volatile and keeps data for the long term.

KindDevicesNotes
MagneticHard disk (HDD), floppy disk, magnetic tapeTape is sequential access, used for backup. A disk is direct (random) access, split into tracks and sectors.
OpticalCD (about 700 MB), DVD (4.7 GB single layer), Blu-ray (25 GB single layer)Read by a laser. Blu-ray uses a blue-violet laser.
Flash (solid state)SSD, pen drive, memory cardNo moving parts, faster than HDD
  • CD-ROM, DVD and Blu-ray are optical, not magnetic.
  • CD-R is write once; CD-RW can be rewritten.
  • Hard disk speed is given in RPM (for example 5400 or 7200).

concepts.title: Data units and address lines
concepts.body:
UnitEqual to
1 nibble4 bits
1 byte8 bits
1 KB (kilobyte)1024 bytes = 210 bytes
1 MB1024 KB = 220 bytes
1 GB1024 MB = 230 bytes
1 TB1024 GB
1 PB, EB, ZB, YBEach 1024 times the one before
  • Order to remember: bit, nibble, byte, KB, MB, GB, TB, PB, EB, ZB, YB.
  • A bit (binary digit) is 0 or 1, the smallest unit. A word is the number of bits the CPU handles at once (32-bit, 64-bit).
  • Bandwidth or bit rate is how much data can move per second, in bits per second (bps, kbps, Mbps, Gbps). Note small b = bits, capital B = bytes.
  • Address lines: n lines can address 2n locations. For a memory of 4K × 8 bits: 4K = 4096 = 212 locations, so 12 address lines; the 8 is the word size, so 8 data lines.

Character codes: ASCII uses 7 bits (128 characters; extended ASCII 8 bits), Unicode covers all languages (UTF-8, UTF-16), EBCDIC is IBM's 8-bit code.

concepts.title: Input and output devices
concepts.body:
InputOutputBoth
Keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone, webcam, joystick, light pen, barcode reader, MICR, OCR, OMR, biometric sensorMonitor, printer, plotter, speaker, headphones, projectorTouch screen, modem, network card
  • MICR (magnetic ink character recognition): reads the magnetic ink numbers on bank cheques.
  • OCR (optical character recognition): turns printed text into editable text.
  • OMR (optical mark recognition): reads filled bubbles on exam answer sheets.
  • A plotter prints large drawings such as maps and building plans. It is an output device.
  • Monitor quality: resolution (pixels, for example 1920 × 1080) and refresh rate (Hz). Types: CRT, LCD, LED.
  • Standard keyboard layout is QWERTY; a full keyboard has 12 function keys (F1 to F12).

concepts.title: Printers and ports
concepts.body:
Impact printers (strike the paper)Non-impact printers (no striking)
Dot matrix, daisy wheel, line printer. Noisy; can print carbon copies. Speed of dot matrix in cps (characters per second); line printer in lpm (lines per minute).Laser, inkjet, thermal. Quiet, better quality. A laser printer uses toner powder and a drum, prints a full page at a time (speed in ppm, pages per minute).
PortWhat it does
Serial (COM, RS-232)Sends one bit at a time in a single stream; slow, but works over long distances (old modems, mouse)
Parallel (LPT)Sends 8 bits at once over short distances; old printers
USBUniversal Serial Bus: plug and play for most devices
VGAAnalog video to a monitor; 15-pin connector in three rows
HDMIDigital audio and video in one cable
PS/2Old 6-pin round port for keyboard and mouse
RJ-45 (Ethernet)Wired network cable

concepts.title: Number systems
concepts.body:
SystemBaseDigits
Binary20, 1
Octal80 to 7
Decimal100 to 9
Hexadecimal160 to 9, A (10) to F (15)
  • Any base to decimal: multiply each digit by baseposition and add. (1011)2 = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11. (2F)16 = 2 × 16 + 15 = 47.
  • Decimal to any base: divide by the base again and again, then read the remainders from bottom to top. 25 in binary = 11001.
  • Binary to octal: group 3 bits from the right. 110 101 = (65)8.
  • Binary to hexadecimal: group 4 bits from the right. 0011 0101 = (35)16.
  • Useful values: 28 = 256, 210 = 1024, (100)10 = (1100100)2 = (144)8 = (64)16.
  • 1's complement: flip every bit. 2's complement: 1's complement plus 1 (used to store negative numbers).

varieties.name: Generations, history and types of computers
varieties.how: Match the technology to the generation: vacuum tube 1st, transistor 2nd, IC 3rd, microprocessor 4th, AI 5th.

example.q: Which generation of computers first used transistors?
steps: Vacuum tubes were used in the first generation.
Transistors replaced them in the second generation (about 1956–1963).

varieties.name: CPU, registers and booting
varieties.how: Learn each register by what it holds: PC next instruction address, IR current instruction, MAR memory address, MDR memory data.

example.q: Which register holds the address of the memory location being accessed?
steps: MDR holds the data, not the address.

varieties.name: Primary memory and the memory hierarchy
varieties.how: RAM is volatile, ROM is not. Cache is SRAM, main memory is DRAM. Order of speed: registers, cache, RAM, secondary storage.

example.q: Which ROM can be erased with ultraviolet light and reprogrammed?
steps: PROM can be written only once.
EPROM is erased with UV light.

varieties.name: Secondary storage devices
varieties.how: Sort the device into magnetic (HDD, floppy, tape), optical (CD, DVD, Blu-ray) or flash (SSD, pen drive).

example.q: Which of these is not a magnetic storage device: hard disk, floppy disk, magnetic tape, CD-ROM?
steps: Hard disk, floppy and tape store data magnetically.
A CD-ROM is read by a laser, so it is optical.

varieties.name: Data units, bit rate and address lines
varieties.how: Each step from KB up is × 1024. For address lines, write the number of locations as a power of 2; the power is the number of lines.

example.q: A memory has a capacity of 4K × 8 bits. How many address lines are needed?
steps: The × 8 is the word size (data lines), not the address.

varieties.name: Input and output devices, ports and printers
varieties.how: Ask which way the data goes: into the computer (input) or out (output). For printers, ask whether it strikes the paper.

example.q: Which device is used by banks to read the numbers printed on cheques?
steps: Cheque numbers are printed in magnetic ink.
Magnetic Ink Character Recognition reads them.

varieties.name: Number system conversions
varieties.how: Go through decimal if unsure. For binary to octal group 3 bits; for binary to hex group 4 bits.

steps: Octal: group 3 bits from the right: 110 | 101 = 6 | 5 = (65)<sub>8</sub>.

tips: Generations in order: vacuum tube, transistor, IC, microprocessor, AI.
Volatile means the data goes when the power goes. Only RAM (and cache, registers) is volatile.
For address lines, write the number of memory locations as 2 to the power n; n is the answer.
MICR is for bank cheques, OMR for exam answer sheets, OCR for turning printed text into editable text.
Binary to octal: groups of 3 bits. Binary to hex: groups of 4 bits. Always group from the right.
A laptop is also called a notebook; a laser printer is a non-impact page printer that uses toner.
traps: 1 KB is 1024 bytes, not 1000, in these questions.
MAR holds an address; MDR holds data. Do not swap them.
CD-ROM, DVD and Blu-ray are optical, not magnetic.
Serial ports send one bit at a time; parallel ports send 8 bits at once.
A plotter is an output device even though it draws.

questions.q: Which part of a computer is called its "brain"?
questions.solution: The Central Processing Unit (CPU) controls and processes all instructions, so it is called the brain of the computer.

questions.q: Which memory loses its contents when the power is switched off?
questions.solution: RAM is volatile memory. ROM, EPROM and hard disk are non-volatile and keep data without power.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an input device?
questions.solution: A plotter draws large graphics on paper, so it is an output device. Scanner, light pen and joystick send data into the computer.

questions.q: Which of these is the fastest memory?
questions.solution: Speed order: Registers > Cache > RAM > SSD. Registers are inside the CPU itself, so they are the fastest.

questions.q: The binary number (1011)<sub>2</sub> is equal to which decimal number?
The hexadecimal number (2F)<sub>16</sub> is equal to which decimal number?
A memory of 4 GB is equal to how many MB?
